title: Token Leakage Channels
description: Ways authentication tokens can escape their intended storage or audience.

attacks.name: Referer leakage
attacks.desc: Tokens placed in URLs can leak to another site through Referer headers when the browser sends the URL.
attacks.prevention: Keep credentials and reset tokens out of URLs, set a strict Referrer-Policy, and avoid third-party content on sensitive pages.

attacks.name: Browser history leakage
attacks.desc: Tokens embedded in visited URLs may remain in local browser history and synchronized records.
attacks.prevention: Use one-time tokens in protected flows rather than URL-bearing long-lived credentials, and remove token parameters from history.

attacks.name: Log file leakage
attacks.desc: Access logs can retain tokens included in URL paths or query strings.
attacks.prevention: Send tokens in protected headers or bodies instead of URLs, and redact secrets from access and application logs.

attacks.name: postMessage token leak
attacks.desc: Sending a token with postMessage to an overly broad target origin can expose it to an unintended window.

attacks.name: Autofill leakage
attacks.desc: Hidden or misplaced fields may receive stored credentials through browser autofill.

attacks.name: Browser sync leakage
attacks.desc: Browser synchronization can carry URLs or other token-bearing data to another signed-in device.

attacks.name: Cache leakage
attacks.desc: Authenticated responses containing tokens can leak through shared caches or browser storage if cache rules are wrong.

attacks.name: Screenshot/OG leakage
attacks.desc: Metadata, previews, or screenshots can capture token-bearing URLs that were intended to stay private.
